title: What should you ask first in a private equity case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in a private equity case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Private equity cases are close cousins of acquisition cases, with a sharper focus on returns and an exit in a few years.
body:
The first question to ask

What return does the fund need, and over how long?

How to build your structure

  • Market (size and growth, margins, barriers to entry)
  • Company (position vs peers, performance, management team)
  • Value creation (revenue growth, margins, add-on deals)
  • Deal (entry price, debt the business can carry)
  • Exit and returns (buyers, exit multiple, money multiple and yearly return vs the fund's target)

The trap most people fall into

No exit thinking.

For the full tree, with every branch, read the private equity framework.

Worked example: why the exit matters

A fund buys a company for £100 million. It invests £40 million of equity and finances the remaining £60 million with debt. Five years later the company is sold for £140 million and outstanding debt is £40 million. Ignoring fees, taxes and interim distributions, equity proceeds are £100 million: £140 million less £40 million debt.

The fund's money multiple is £100 million ÷ £40 million = 2.5×. Its approximate annualised return is (2.5)^(1/5) − 1, or about 20%. The purchase may look excellent on operating profit and still fail if the fund overpays, debt cannot be serviced or an attractive exit is unavailable.

Work backward from the fund's minimum acceptable return. Stress-test a lower exit multiple, slower earnings growth, higher debt at exit and a later sale date. Keep enterprise value, debt and equity value separate. A private-equity answer needs both a plan to improve the business and a convincing path to cash proceeds for equity investors.
